title: OpenAI's unreleased Astra model solves ten decade-old math problems, publishes Lean proofs
subtitle: The company's next major model family, previewed to senators before the public, produced formal machine-verified solutions to open questions in group theory, coding theory and high-dimensional geometry — for about $2,000 in tokens.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: On August 1, OpenAI published ten mathematical results generated by an internal version of Astra, the model family it has been describing as its next major release. The proofs cover open problems in group theory, coding theory, quantum complexity, and high-dimensional geometry, and each was formalized in Lean — a proof assistant that mechanically checks every step — before publication. The company estimates the API-equivalent token cost at roughly $2,000, using rates comparable to its current Sol-class endpoints. The manuscripts and Lean scripts were posted to GitHub.

The headline result is a construction of a non-sofic group, resolving a question posed by Mikhail Gromov in 1999 that had stood untouched for twenty-seven years. Other outputs include new sphere-packing bounds in high dimensions and progress on quantum complexity separations. Fields Medalist Timothy Gowers told reporters he would recommend one of the proofs to a top journal without hesitation. The choice to release formal Lean proofs rather than natural-language write-ups is what makes the results reviewable at all — a human referee cannot yet audit ten decade-open problems overnight, but a Lean kernel can verify each proof in seconds.

Astra itself is positioned as a multi-agent system designed to work on a single problem for hours or days, with several agents planning, delegating, and revising against a shared goal. Sam Altman spent July 29 in closed-door meetings with senators and administration officials in Washington — including Sens. Raphael Warnock and Bernie Moreno, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick — demonstrating the system before the public reveal. The model has not been released to the public, and OpenAI has said Astra will be the first family to go through the voluntary pre-release review framework established under Executive Order 14409, which requires a thirty-day government window before general availability.

For learners: the interesting signal here is not 'AI can do math now.' It is that OpenAI paired a hard-to-fake capability demonstration with a public, machine-verifiable artifact and a private policy demonstration on the same weekend. Frontier AI has moved into a regime where capability announcements and government engagement are the same announcement. When you evaluate any research claim like this one, look for two things — a formal verification path (here, Lean) and independent expert commentary (here, Gowers). Press releases don't tell you what a model can do; artifacts and reviewers do.
